text: Walt, to Mr. Lin, not looking up: "You moved the horse like it was a xiangqi horse again." Mr. Lin: "Because it's better." Walt laughs, which he almost never does.
Gary, on his phone by the fence: "Half the signs at the clinic are in Chinese now. I'm just saying the people who've lived here forty years should get a say."
Sunday dinner at Mr. Guo's. Eight people around a lazy Susan, festival budgets on a legal pad between the dishes. He seats you next to the treasurer and says, "Learn from her."
choice1: Stay late and help with the budget.

text: Thursday potluck in the library basement. Ruth seats you with a family from Fuzhou and a retired mailman. By dessert the mailman is learning to count to ten in Mandarin.
The association meeting: twelve folding chairs, a coffee urn, forty minutes on the Fifth Street lot. When someone says "those people", Gary changes the subject without looking at you.
choice2: Sit quietly and leave at the break.

text: The joint health fair. Dr. Zhou takes blood pressures at one table, Ruth signs people up for benefits at the next. You spend the morning walking seniors from the center through the library's front door.
Your family group chat, 6:40 a.m.: a forwarded video of agents checking IDs at a subway entrance. Your aunt adds, in all caps, a reminder to carry your passport.
choice2: Mute the chat for the day.

text: The intake form has a new line: 'Citizenship status (required for federal reporting).' The receptionist says quietly, "You can leave it blank. I didn't write that rule."
choice2: Fill it in and hand it back.

text: A local news alert: the Fifth Street Clinic will have Mandarin and Cantonese interpreters on site three days a week starting Monday, under the new federal rule. "Ask at the desk, in any language," says the director, Dr. Nadia Haddad.
Dr. Zhou is pinning a notice to the board: 'New: free help with citizenship applications. Library and Center, together.' She steps back to check it's straight.

Morning radio: a Guatemalan family two neighborhoods over was detained at a routine check-in. Their kids went to school at PS 21, where Mrs. Chen's grandson goes. The principal, Karen Novak, says counselors will be in every classroom today.

Morning radio, the governor's call-in hour. Dale Whitaker says state troopers will "help our federal partners" with ID checks on the interstate. A caller asks about people whose applications are still pending. "If your paperwork's in order, you've got nothing to worry about."

A letter is taped inside the reception window, signed by the director, Dr. Nadia Haddad: 'This clinic does not ask about immigration status and does not share your records with anyone who is not treating you.' Someone has underlined 'anyone' in blue pen.
choice1: Take a photo of it for your family.

text: A note from PS 21 goes round your building's group chat. The principal, Karen Novak: parent-teacher night now has interpreters for Mandarin, Spanish and Bengali, "just tell the front desk which." Someone replies: "Finally. Last year I nodded for an hour."
choice1: Forward it to your cousin with kids.

text: Dana waves you over and slides a book across the desk: a cookbook from the Sichuan place on Grand that closed in 2019. "Found it in donations. You said you missed their fish."
Mrs. Chen hands you an apron. "Seniors' lunch, sixty people, two volunteers sick. You fold, I'll boil." The dumpling wrappers are already counted into stacks of twenty.
Mr. Guo, to the room, not quite to you: "Some young people come here once a month, like visiting a museum." A couple of the aunties look at their teacups.
choice2: Say nothing and help stack chairs.

text: Jia drops a container of frozen dumplings on your desk. "My mom made two hundred. I'm outsourcing. Don't tell her, she'll ask what you thought."
A manager from another team, after your presentation: "Your English is really good, by the way. Where are you from originally?" You've lived in this city longer than he has.
Mr. Lin has drawn a xiangqi river in chalk across the stone board and is showing Walt how the elephant can't cross it. Walt says it's a stupid rule. He keeps playing.
choice1: Pull up a seat and coach Walt.

text: A voice message from your mom: she's making zongzi this weekend and wants to know how many to save you. Then, as an afterthought, whether you've called your grandmother.

Nine a.m. on the roof. Dana has two folding chairs, a thermos, and an empty pot with 3B written on it in marker, waiting for spring. Mr. Ortiz comes up at ten and tells you both the pots are in the wrong corner.
choice1: Stay and help move the pots.
choice2: Finish your coffee and head down.
